articles.title: Vatican says Pope Leo will be released from hospital Saturday, 4 days after cancer surgery
articles.summary: VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is being released from the hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery , and will deliver the traditional noon blessing Sunday from a window overlooking St. Peter's Square, the Vatican announced. The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma , the most common type of lung cancer. His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was “deemed fit for discharge from the hospital” based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, along with an assessment of his clinical condition. He is set to leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican, the Vatican said in a brief statement. With notable transparency, Leo announced last Sunday to the faithful gathered in St. Peter’s Square that doctors had identified a nodule on his lung, and that it would be removed. Since the surgery on Tuesday that confirmed the cancer diagnosis, Leo has given strong indications that he was recovering well, including by holding a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meeting with top aides and celebrating Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel. Medical bulletins from his personal physician and surgeon likewise indicated a good post-operative recovery that had allowed him to carry on “normal daily activities completely on his own.” The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him standing up at an altar in a hospital chapel in green vestments, as doctors said that tests confirmed his “continued improvement.” Leo presided alone over the liturgy, distributing Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present, Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said. He also delivered a homily in which he thanked the hospital staff “for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him,” Bruni said. The Vatican had originally estimated a weeklong hospital stay, and canceled his audiences through Tuesday. Experts indicated that patients could be discharged earlier depending on the pace of their recovery, and Bruni said the discharge date was up to the pope's doctors. The pope’s next big agenda item is a trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17, which gives Leo three more weeks of recovery before taking on the ambitious journey that includes a dozen flights and two helicopter trips. The Vatican has given signs of all-systems go, publishing the names of journalists accredited to fly on Leo’s plane on Friday. And oncology surgeons say protocols generally clear patients to fly after three weeks, as long as recovery allows. Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary. articles.title: An armed dad and a teacher stopped an Oregon school shooter. It took just 3 minutes.
articles.summary: Community members grieve at the site of a makeshift memorial in front of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on October 16. - Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images On a sunny Oregon fall morning, parents dressed their children up and sent them to Silver Rail Elementary School for picture day. It’s the kind of picture parents return to years later, marveling at how small their children once were and how their smiles looked before their faces changed. But for some families, snapshots in their minds from that morning will carry a devastating, final memory of a child who never came home. Just hours after Steven and Angela Nuchols sent their 8-year-old daughter to school, they raced back to Silver Rail, desperate to know whether she was alive, they told local news outlet , The Bend Source . “It was crawling with police officers from all over the county,” Angela Nuchols told The Bend Source . “You’ve got guys in tactical gear, rifles. You’re just scared to death wondering, is your child OK?” For the Nuchols family, the next few hours before they were reunited with their daughter at a church were “the worst three hours of our lives,” Angela said. American schools have repeatedly seen the illusion of safety shattered within the walls of their classrooms. An elementary school in Bend, Oregon, was the latest among them, when a 16-year-old opened fire on Thursday, killing three children, including Rhoam Summer, aged 5; and two others, aged 8 and 11; as well as a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, police said. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were injured and taken to local hospitals, according to officials. Another school turned into a crime scene; a violation of the sanctity of childhood. A drone view shows Silver Rail Elementary School, the day after a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 16. - David Ryder/Reuters 180 seconds of terror Michelle was a freshman in high school in California when she survived a school shooting in 2001. The trauma followed her into adulthood; she learned to scan rooms for exits, sit facing doors and live with anxiety and panic attacks. Long before the shooting, every school drop-off carried a quiet dread. Michelle, who is withholding her last name for privacy, would watch her children go, a pit in her stomach, wondering whether she would see them again. Then, on Thursday, her fifth-grade son called from Silver Rail Elementary School. “Mom, there’s a shooter.” Michelle was eating at an Olive Garden when her son’s voice came through his Apple Watch. She cried while recounting the moment, and said she immediately knew from the sound of his voice that something was terribly wrong. She told him she loved him, urged him to stay quiet and hung up to call 911. As she ran to her car, the call rang without an answer. She raced toward the school, about 10 minutes away. “I was like, how can this happen?” Michelle wonders, her voice shaking. “How can lightning strike twice?” A mother who lived through a 2001 school shooting comforts her son during Silver Rail Elementary shooting. - Michelle The first 911 call came at 12:59 p.m., after the driver of a red pickup truck saw a man approach the school, throw his long gun over the fence and climb over after it, police said Friday. When the pickup driver confronted him, the suspect opened fire, striking the truck at least three times. From her classroom window, fifth-grade teacher Kathy Sheil Smith watched the gunman walk toward the building. She called the main office, then pulled her students into a corner. “They were so afraid. The looks on their faces, it was really hard to see,” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV, trying to hold back tears. “Some kids were praying, some kids were consoling other kids. But they were doing so quietly because they know you don’t make any noise.” She wondered whether she would live to see the end of the day. What mattered to her was that her students would. “I’m sure that every teacher at the school thought, ‘Today is the day that I am going to die,’” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV . “Save my kids.” As Smith tried to shield her students inside the school, a terrifying picture was emerging. Around 12:59 p.m., emergency dispatchers received a flood of calls reporting that a person had entered the Silver Rail Elementary School and started shooting, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz. At 1:01 p.m., police directed the school to go into lockdown. “Ms. Hawkins, the principal, was saying ‘lockdown, lockdown,’ and then the shots kept on going and going,” one 9-year-old student told CNN affiliate KGW , describing how he hid under a sink for 30 minutes, fearing the gunman would approach his classroom next. “I’m pretty sure a girl. She was saying, ‘Please, please, no,’ and then it was a shot and then dead silence,” he added. The gunman went directly into the classroom just left of the entrance and fired as many as 15 rounds, according to Krantz. The classroom was dedicated to special needs students, according to Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook. A second driver, a 36-year-old father whose children attend the school, had witnessed the initial shooting, drove into the school parking lot and followed the suspect into the school with his legally secured 40-caliber pistol, police said. The bystander was identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco on Friday. A teacher — who was not injured — threw her cellphone at the shooter and tackled him in an attempt to get the gun away from him, the police chief said. When Giamanco heard gunfire and saw the teacher physically struggling with the gunman, Giamanco entered the classroom and fired, striking the suspect multiple times and killing him, police said. Less than half a mile away, business owner Sierra Jordan told CNN the familiar sound of children laughing and playing outside at recess gave way to the frantic arrival of ambulances. About three minutes after the first 911 call, it was over: At 1:02 p.m., police arrived and reported the shooter had been shot and killed by Giamanco. President Donald Trump called Giamanco “a great hero” who “took care of business.” “Had this not happened, had the bystander not neutralized the shooter? This could have been a much more tragic event than it was,” former FBI special agent Ken Gray told CNN. The shooter was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former special needs student at the school, Krantz said Friday. A Maverick 88 pump-action, 12-gauge shotgun was found near the suspect, who had about 44 remaining rounds of 12-gauge ammunition, Krantz added. The gun had been purchased by his mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN earlier Friday. Tragedy plunges community into grief Bend, a picturesque city of about 100,000 people, sits in the high desert landscape of central Oregon. It is a city of sage-scented air, snow-capped peaks and the Deschutes River that cuts through the heart of downtown; a magnet for thrill-seekers finding solace in the nearby mountain trails, red rock cliffs and star-filled skies. Although the city has boomed in recent years, it remains a quiet corner of the American West where the wilderness begins just beyond the city streets and its brick front stores and breweries. “Bend is a place that people move to from bigger cities,” Former Bend Mayor Jeff Eager told CNN . “They move here because it’s relatively safe here; they move here because we have schools you can walk your kids to,” Eager said. “You can’t imagine that it happens here.” But against Bend’s picturesque backdrop, the aftermath looked devastatingly familiar. Parents rushing to a reunification center, hearts clenched with the hope of finding their children among the survivors. Police tape cordoned off the school as officers stood guard. An emergency worker holds up police tape at the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, October 15. - Rob Kerr/Reuters The minutes had passed so quickly for the rest of the world, but for the families waiting to learn whether their children were alive, the abrupt end of the gunfire wasn’t the end of their agony. The prevalence of school shootings in America should prompt a conversation about “responsible gun ownership,” Democratic Rep. Janelle Bynum of Oregon told CNN. “This school, we had invested money in to make sure that it was locked. They did all of their drills as expected — everything that we’ve said that will protect kids up to now, and yet it didn’t work,” she said. “The laws don’t go far enough, fast enough for us to be able to intervene,” Bynum said. “We have to stop allowing our children to be shredded in schools, grocery stores, parks, churches. We have to stop this violence.” Investigators seek answers The Bend-La Pine school district — of which Silver Rail Elementary School is part — has multiple security measures in place such as secure entry vestibules, photo ID checks and visitor screenings, indoor and outdoor security cameras and upgraded locks on classroom doors that can be secured from inside, according to the district. Despite those measures, some of which were upgraded in 2022, the gunman was able to force his way into the elementary school by shooting at locked doors. It is not yet clear why the shooter was able to bypass security measures, the district’s superintendent said. Investigators are still working to establish a motive for the shooting, authorities said Friday. A search warrant was executed at the alleged shooter’s house on Thursday, according to a senior law enforcement official, who told CNN c omputers and other electronics were taken. Search warrants have also been obtained to gain access to the devices and extract data, according to the source. Local law enforcement and the FBI will examine the material for evidence that could help explain what led to the shooting. The shooter’s parents were cooperative and told investigators their son had attended Silver Rail Elementary School during their interview, the source said. During the pandemic, the shooter’s mother spoke with CNN affiliate KTVZ about her hopes that in-person classes would resume for children with special needs. The program was described as serving children with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.” She spoke briefly with CNN off camera from her balcony on Friday but declined to comment on how her son got access to the weapon. Authorities say that is still under investigation. The woman told CNN there were no warning signs. “I miss my boy. I’m so sorry,” the woman said as she cried and smoked a cigarette. In a message to the families of those killed, she said: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.” Another chorus of thoughts and prayers Members of the Bend community gathered downtown in Drake Park on Thursday evening for a prayer vigil to support each other and grieve. Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler spoke while in tears alongside Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, who was also crying. A large crowd of mourners held candles and hugged one another as they listened to prayers, music and community leaders. People wrote tributes in chalk. “NEVER again,” one person wrote. “Be at peace,” scribbled another. A young child knelt to place a lit candle on a step. By Friday, a makeshift memorial had taken shape outside Silver Rail Elementary School. Bouquets of flowers, toys and red, heart-shaped balloons lined a nearby crosswalk, just beyond yellow police tape. One mother, Ally Land, brought her children, 8 and 5, to the memorial. Her children don’t attend Silver Rail, but Land said she wanted to help them understand what had happened, answering their questions as best she could. “I asked them what they knew, and they just said, ‘I know that school’s canceled, so that they can make school safer tomorrow,’” Land told CNN . “We told them something terrible had happened, and we just followed their questions from there.” All Bend-La Pine Schools were closed on Friday, including activities and athletic events, the district said. But a day without classes cannot prevent the next shooting. The Silver Rail Elementary tragedy is the 36th shooting in the United States this year on K-12 school grounds, according to CNN’s analysis of multiple databases, including the Gun Violence Archive. “As a country, we still lack the courage to do anything to try to prevent these things from occurring,” CNN’s Senior Law Enforcement Analyst Charles Ramsey told CNN’s Elex Michaelson on Friday. “And it’s going to happen again.” Blake and Danielle Brinker were at their home outside Bend with Blake’s mother when they learned of the shooting, they told CNN. Blake said, describing his emotions at the time, as “just absolutely gutted.” The pair, who know people directly affected by the shooting, also visited the memorial. “Immediately could feel the energy of the community just stop on a dime,” Blake said. Danielle described Bend as “a very magical place.” A woman lights a candle during a candlelight vigil at Drake Park for victims of the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 15. - David Ryder/Reuters The town was named in the top 75 safest midsize cities in the country, according to a SmartAsset study earlier this year. But Thursday’s deadly shooting isn’t the first in Bend. In 2022, a 20-year-old gunman, a Bend resident, killed two people after walking into a grocery store with an AR-15-style rifle and opening fire. Back in Bend, Cook, the district superintendent at Bend-La Pine Schools, spent Friday with staff at the school who are grappling with the devastating aftermath. “They are in so much pain, as we all are,” Cook said. “This has been a terrifying and traumatic experience that will affect us all profoundly for years to come.” Michelle, the 2001 school shooting survivor and a mother of children at Silver Rail Elementary School, carried for years the knowledge that gun violence could shatter an ordinary day without warning. But she’d hoped her children would never have to know what that’s like. “My friend said to me, this is generational trauma, this is a second generation that’s been through school shooting trauma,” Michelle told CNN. “How sick is that?” CNN’s Taylor Galgano, Helen Regan, Emma Tucker, Norma Galeana, Caroll Alvarado, Alisha Ebrahimji, Amanda Jackson, Leigh Waldman, John Miller, Rebekah Riess and Elise Hammond contributed to this report. articles.title: Katie Zacharia reportedly out as White House press secretary after first week on the job
articles.summary: President Trump’s embattled new press secretary Katie Zacharia was forced out Friday after less than a week on the job. “It was an honor to work for him,” Zacharia wrote on social media , confirming widespread reports that Trump had let her go. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung told CNN in a statement that Zacharia “will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role.” Zacharia is the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history. Earlier Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia was on her way out, telling reporters that he had asked Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this." "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said. Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media." Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News, Politico and the Washington Post published similar reports. Trump: "I told Katie that in my opinion she was treated very very unfairly by the news. Let's call it the fake news. I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.' We're talking about doing something. I want her to have a good life. She's being brutalized by the… pic.twitter.com/Ivkk5imCjS — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 16, 2026 The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August. Zacharia started at the White House on Monday gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda. In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. In media appearances, Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia." Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China." In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper.  "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One.  And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question." Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time. On Thursday, Zacharia confimed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China." On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer." White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added. Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law." "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice,"  she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'" On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation . "Why not just say, 'I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. "Why get into this long drawn-out thing about the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?" "When I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar," Zacharia said. "I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law." What happened in Zacharia's first briefing? White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the  Briefing Room on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement. "I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time." She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing. Asked what she planned to do as press secretary, Zacharia said, "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was getting to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people." In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump said Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on X . Who is Katie Zacharia? President Donald Trump and Katie Zacharia. Katie Zacharia/X The 42-year-old California native and mother of four left her role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, to join the White House. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn profile . She was best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol." Zacharia first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California with her husband and their four young children. During Tuesday's briefing, she was asked about juggling the competing roles of being a mother and White House press secretary. "The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia said, before confusing her spouse with her boss. "So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here." Zacharia then praised Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had" and said her family will be moving from California to Washington, D.C., soon. CNN reported on Friday that Zacharia's "selection came about quickly" and that she "was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position." In a New York Post column in February , Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class. "I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent." articles.title: Trump pauses Russia sanctions passed by Congress, citing U.S. national interest
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats. Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham , the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine . Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia. An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3. Sanctions were seen as part of Graham's legacy Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine. His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday. The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving. It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.” “These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said. Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had “warned" Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine.” The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress. Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting. The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy. Trump's action follows announced diesel deal with Putin Under last week's agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Trump’s striking a diesel deal with Putin has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran. The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham , the late senator’s sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently. Darline Graham said in a statement after Trump signed the bill, “I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day." In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed. She acknowledged, however, that it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it. “It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-puts-russia-sanctions-passed-014202867.html

articles.title: FEMA lays groundwork to shift disaster burden to states
articles.summary: The Trump administration plans to reduce state and local dependency on federal disaster aid and could move Federal Emergency Management Agency workers out of Washington, D.C., according to an internal FEMA memo obtained by POLITICO. FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton wrote in an Oct. 15 memo — confirmed by two people with direct knowledge of it — that the agency will “strengthen state and local emergency management capacity” in an effort to lower reliance on the federal government. “Reducing federal dependency requires partners to build, maintain, and exercise the capabilities needed to manage incidents effectively,” the seven-page memo to agency employees says. In a separate section, the memo says, “FEMA must reduce unnecessary centralization in Washington, D.C.,” and that “regional and field teams are often closest to disaster survivors, state and local officials, emergency managers, and community partners.” The memo is the clearest indication that the administration will follow through on President Donald Trump’s long-stated desire to shift disaster management to states and reduce the federal role in preparation and recovery. It’s also the first indication of Hamilton’s priorities since he became the first permanent FEMA administrator in Trump’s second term in August. A series of acting leaders had run FEMA since January 2025, and their temporary status precluded the agency from making structural changes. Although Trump has called for weakening FEMA since his first week in office, no new policies emerged, creating uncertainty about the future of federal disaster aid. Trump has indirectly discouraged reliance on federal disaster aid by taking far longer than his predecessors — including Trump in his first term — to act on state requests for help after major storms, floods, wildfires and other disasters. Hamilton’s memo echoes recommendations of a Trump-appointed FEMA review panel to build state and local capacity and make it harder for states to qualify for federal disaster aid. The memo also has general language about “eliminating unnecessary steps, reducing administrative burden” and taking other action to expedite and simplify FEMA’s notoriously slow and laborious process of approving aid. Shana Udvardy of the Union of Concerned Scientists said she worries that the memo “seems to promote efficiency and accountability over the welfare of communities.” “When you have a lot of focus on accountability and efficiency, you’re going to have staff losing focus on the bigger picture of resiliency,” said Udvardy, UCS’ senior climate policy resilience analyst. “It’s really hard to know what this is going to look like in practice.” FEMA did not respond to a request for comment on the memo. The agency has limited ability to revise its own policies, which are mostly set by federal law. Congress hasn’t changed FEMA operations significantly since 2018, and congressional leaders have shown little interest in bipartisan legislation to overhaul the agency. Hamilton says in his memo that the objectives he outlined “will guide FEMA’s planning, budgeting, program management, operations, and partner engagement. Each office, region, and program must assess whether its current activities align with these priorities and identify opportunities to improve execution.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/16/fema-state-reliance-federal-aid-01124455

articles.title: DOJ warns California election officials of possible prosecution over noncitizen votes
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month's midterm election, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. The letter Friday from a senior Justice Department official and obtained first by The Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. “The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department. It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.” The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. In response to the letter, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away. “The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court,” he said. The other offices and the state attorney general did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It is unclear how many individuals the Justice Department might look to try to investigate and charge, though any federal criminal cases in the Los Angeles area would be handled by the office of Bill Essayli, the region's top federal prosecutor and one of the Justice Department officials who filed the federal complaint Thursday against California. Trump weighed in late Friday, sharing on Truth Social a link to a news story about the letter and adding: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!” The Trump administration has made the pursuit of noncitizen voters a priority Sent less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the letter adds to simmering tensions over voter rolls between California and the Justice Department and reflects the Trump administration's aggressive hunt for noncitizen voters . It has made the issue a priority this year, including by demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens . There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state. That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero. That experience is backed up by research and investigations in various states, which make clear that voting by noncitizens is extremely rare. The letter follows a Justice Department lawsuit The Justice Department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given , and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter “ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution.” “It is deplorable that rather than work cooperatively and assist states in their election administration responsibilities, the federal government is making escalating threats and unreasonable demands beyond its power in the middle of an ongoing election,” he said. Justin Levitt, a former deputy assistant attorney general who teaches at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, dismissed the idea that an attempted prosecution of an election official using the letter’s rationale would hold up. “Courts haven’t been buying what DOJ has been selling, and nothing in this letter is calibrated to change course,” he said. “Fortunately, election officials — not just in Los Angeles, but across the country — are equipped to stand up to aggressive bullying. And the law is on their side.” Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. The Trump administration's escalating threats against California come as Democratic lawmakers are urging the Justice Department to honor its longstanding policy of not interfering in U.S. elections. Earlier Friday, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Dick Durbin, D-Il., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified. ___ Associated Press writers Michael R. Blood in Los Angeles and Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report. articles.title: Judge threatens to sanction Trump for delaying deposition in $10 billion BBC case
articles.summary: Topline A federal magistrate judge threatened Friday to levy sanctions against President Donald Trump for failing to “participate” in his own defamation lawsuit against the BBC, after the broadcaster informed the court that Trump had backed out of a planned deposition in the case and suggested he couldn’t be interviewed until next year. President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn as he departs the White House on October 12 in Washington, DC. Getty Images Key Facts Magistrate Judge Enjolique A. Lett issued an order Friday directing Trump to file a response to the BBC regarding his deposition by Oct. 22, noting the court had already “admonished” the president for his “lack of participation” in the case “to no avail.” Failing to “strict[ly]” comply with the court’s schedule for discovery in the case, Lett wrote Friday, “will lead to sanctions.” Trump has sued the BBC for $10 billion, claiming the broadcaster allegedly defamed him by “deceptively” editing a video of the president’s speech on Jan. 6, 2021 for a 2024 documentary, in order to falsely suggest Trump was trying to incite violence on Jan. 6 and bias viewers against him in the 2024 election. As part of discovery in the lawsuit—where both sides gather evidence to support their case—the BBC is trying to get a deposition from Trump, which it said in a filing Tuesday was supposed to take place Friday. After first failing to coordinate with the BBC about the logistics for the deposition, Trump’s lawyers told the broadcaster the president wouldn’t be able to attend the deposition because of “other matters of national importance,” and wouldn’t be available to testify until January 2027 at the earliest—despite discovery in the case being scheduled to end in December. Trump’s legal team did not directly respond to the threat of sanctions or the BBC’s request for the court to force Trump to be deposed, but alleged in a statement to Forbes that the president’s lawsuit “is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference.” What to Watch for The BBC has asked the court to compel Trump to be deposed in the case in a reasonable timeframe, and Lett agreed Friday to discuss the issue at a hearing on Oct. 22. It remains to be seen if the judge could levy any sanctions against Trump or his attorneys, and what those punishments could look like if so. Crucial Quote The BBC noted in its filing Tuesday that the court “has been required to intervene at every juncture to cajole even the most basic participation in the discovery process out of” Trump, quoting a past case that argued it’s “not the court’s role, nor that of opposing counsel, to drag a party kicking and screaming through the discovery process,” especially when Trump “was the party which filed this lawsuit” in the first place. The president “chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s attorneys argued to the court. Tangent The debate over Trump’s deposition is one of several taking place in the BBC case, as the broadcaster is also seeking testimony from Trump allies like his children Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump and son-in-law Jared Kushner. The BBC told the court in August that it had so far been blocked from serving subpoenas to the president’s family members in person because of their Secret Service protection, claiming the subpoenas were necessary because the Trump children and Kushner have “personal knowledge” of Trump’s “intention” behind his Jan. 6 speech. The court ruled in October that the broadcaster could instead serve the Trump family through alternate means—like sending a certified letter or contacting their attorneys—paving the way for those depositions to take place. The BBC was less successful in getting a deposition from former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson , who assisted Trump’s then-chief of staff Mark Meadows on Jan. 6 and has testified to Congress about the attack on the Capitol. Hutchinson asked the court to throw out her subpoena, and the court agreed , siding with Hutchinson’s argument that her testimony would be “irrelevant” and would “subject her to oppression and harassment.” Key Background Trump sued the BBC for defamation in December over its 2024 “Panorama” documentary, which aired in the U.K. before the 2024 election, but did not air in the U.S. The documentary quoted the president as telling supporters on Jan. 6, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol... and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell.” In actuality, Trump said, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol, and we’re going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women.” He then made the comment to “fight like hell” more than 50 minutes later. The BBC has apologized to the president for the editing job, saying it gave “the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action,” but has strongly denied it was defamatory. While Trump initially argued the BBC’s editing job had hurt his businesses, the lawsuit now only argues that it harmed his personal reputation, as the court allowed the president to narrow his lawsuit after the BBC asked Trump to turn over significant financial information about his assets and the value of his businesses. articles.title: U.S. deficit nears $2 trillion as government spending keeps climbing
articles.summary: The US federal budget deficit for 2026 officially came in Friday at $1.992 trillion, a final tabulation to close out the government's fiscal year and another reminder of Washington's spiraling reliance on red ink. This deficit number represents about 6% of the US gross domestic product and was a result of $5.403 trillion in total revenues for the fiscal year against total spending of $7.396 trillion. The 2026 reading is a 12% jump from 2025's $1.775 trillion deficit. These final numbers came in the Treasury Department's Monthly Statement for September, which covers the final month in the US government's fiscal calendar. The red ink has led to dire warnings from economists that the US now routinely runs annual deficits that were previously seen only during recessions and wars. The gross US national debt passed $40 trillion in August and now sits above $40.3 trillion. The latest "Debt to the Penny" reading from the Treasury Department came this past Wednesday, putting the gross US national debt at $40,329,229,827,541.02. A bus shelter in Washington display the US National debt in August. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for the Peter G. Peterson Foundation) Jemal Countess via Getty Images Read more: How the soaring federal debt affects you personally The independent budget hawks at the Committee for a Responsible Budget noted in a recent analysis that "the country's future fiscal outlook is even more dismal," noting that annual deficits could reach $3.1 trillion by 2036 without a change in the fiscal trajectory. The group noted that annual interest costs on the debt are now $1.1 trillion, a record 3.4% of GDP, making it the second-largest line item in the government's budget. Interest on the debt still costs less than Social Security , but it is now more expensive than either Medicare or the defense budget. Members of President Trump's team have tried to downplay this year's tabulation — the highest annual deficit reading other than 2020 and 2021, when budgets were inflated by COVID-era spending — as a blip and insist that the US fiscal situation is getting under control. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has focused on the Supreme Court-ordered tariff refunds that have turned a revenue stream into a cost center for the government in recent months. Indeed, the impact of tariff refunds has been significant: $144.6 billion in tariff refunds were given out over the past year — but analyses of the deficit also show a variety of factors that have driven up deficits. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and President Trump are seen during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 7. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images A Hamilton Project tracker of government expenditures shows how government spending has increased at a steady pace in 2026. The tracker looks at spending by calendar year and shows that as of Oct. 14, government spending has jumped each of the last three years. At this point in 2024 — the last year of Joe Biden's presidency — the government had spent $5.76 trillion. On Oct. 14, 2025, spending had grown to $6.13 trillion. So far this year, the government has spent $6.65 trillion. One of the drivers, a Bloomberg Government analysis found, is spending on Trump administration priorities, especially the Department of Homeland Security, whose budget is up 146% from 2025 to 2026. Revenue downturn The revenue side of the US government's budget equation has also faltered on some fronts in 2026, in part due to tax cuts implemented by Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill." A monthly budget review from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) released last week noted that tariff revenues declined, as did corporate income tax collections. The group calculates that corporate income taxes decreased by 16% in 2026 as the new tax cuts allowed corporations to take larger deductions "and offset the increases in those receipts that otherwise would have been expected, given the rise in corporate income." Tariffs were also a significant factor, with the Supreme Court's decision in February striking down Trump's tariffs leading to a refund process in the months that followed that has made tariffs barely a profitable undertaking for the government in 2026. The $144.6 billion in tariff refunds nearly halved the gross receipts of $317.8 billion. And at least some additional tariff refunds could be seen in the months ahead, with the government recently launching "Phase 3" of the refund process . This turnabout in tariffs led to a deficit approximately $140 billion higher than projections from just a few months ago. In February, before the tariff refunds were ordered, the CBO projected a $1.85 trillion annual deficit for this year. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: A powerful El Niño could disrupt winter getaways. Here's what travelers should know.
articles.summary: As travelers look to escape the cold for warm weather over the holiday season, an unusually strong El Niño could lead to unseasonal weather in several popular vacation destinations. The climate pattern, which occurs when waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, can shift weather patterns across the country, potentially affecting popular winter getaways from Florida to the Caribbean. "El Niños are associated with more storminess across the southern tier of the country, and potentially more ice storms across the southern plains," Matthew Rosencrans, a meteorologist at NOAA's Weather Prediction Center, told Yahoo. Those conditions can significantly disrupt travel, the meteorologist said, but the effects will be far from uniform. El Niño winters are also often warmer, Rosencrans explained, which can sometimes benefit travel across the northern tier of the contiguous U.S. Meanwhile, parts of the Caribbean may see drier weather, creating very different conditions for travelers depending on their destination. Where winter travelers could feel the effects Travelers heading to Florida this winter for a holiday getaway could face wetter-than-usual conditions, with El Niño increasing the likelihood of rainfall and severe weather across parts of the Southeast. "For Florida, it often means a fairly robust secondary severe weather season in November and into December across the Southeast and Florida," Rosencrans told Yahoo. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center outlook , released Oct. 15, gives the Southeast and Florida the greatest likelihood of a wetter-than-normal winter, with odds above 70% in some parts of northern Florida through the January to March period. Temperatures are forecast to be near normal across much of the Southeast. The winter seasonal precipitation outlook, according to NOAA. NOAA That doesn't necessarily mean travelers need to rethink a Florida vacation, but those hoping for uninterrupted beach weather should keep an eye on the forecast. While Florida could see a wetter winter, the Caribbean islands may see less rain, though it varies by island and time of year. "The Caribbean can often see drier weather during El Niño events, more strongly in the summer months from reduced tropical activity," Rosencrans explained. The ABC islands, Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao, are one example of where less rain is likely. Their main rainy season typically runs from October through January, with the dry season arriving later, from February through May. An El Niño suppresses that rainy season, according to the Meteorological Department of Curaçao . While lower rainfall over the islands may sound appealing, Rosencrans said it can mean fewer thunderstorms and make days feel hotter "as there is less cloudiness and continuous sunshine." Other islands show no clear lean either way. NOAA's winter outlook , released Oct. 15, gives Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands "equal chances of below-average, near-average or above-average seasonal total precipitation amounts" for December through February. Could El Niño affect hurricane season? El Niño has helped suppress Atlantic hurricane activity this year, but that doesn't mean the threat of tropical storms has disappeared. This year, Isaias became the first Atlantic hurricane of the season late on Oct. 7, making it one day shy of tying a 121-year-old record for the basin's latest-forming hurricane, according to the Associated Press . Lindsey Long, a meteorologist at NOAA's Weather Prediction Center, told Yahoo that wind shear linked to El Niño is still inhibiting storm development across the Atlantic. "In a typical year, we would expect about two additional hurricanes to develop between mid-October and November 30," Long said. By mid-October, the Atlantic would typically have had at least five, according to the National Hurricane Center , as reported by NPR . This year, Isaias is the first. However, the Gulf has been less affected by that wind shear and has extremely warm surface waters that could fuel storms, Long said. Formation typically shifts from the Atlantic's main development region, which stretches from the Caribbean to the African coast, toward the Gulf at this time of year. "There is still a continued possibility for tropical development throughout the remainder of the season," Long told Yahoo. The expert did add that a possible shift in when hurricane season starts or ends would not be connected to El Niño. Travelers heading to hurricane-prone areas may want to consider flexible booking options and review their travel insurance policies to understand what weather-related disruptions are covered. articles.title: IMF警告日本可能需要更快加息，全球债市再添压力？
articles.summary: 国际货币基金组织罕见地为日本货币政策正常化背书，并警告若通胀超预期，日本央行可能需要加快加息步伐。这一表态，在全球债市已然动荡之际，令市场对日本资金撤离海外资产的担忧进一步升温。 IMF亚太部门主任Krishna Srinivasan在本周于曼谷召开的IMF年会期间接受路透社采访时表示， 日本央行"正在做正确的事"，并强调若通胀上升快于预期，"必须更快收紧，因为你不希望通胀预期脱锚。这取决于数据。" 日本央行行长植田和男亦在出席本次IMF年会时重申，央行将专注于将核心通胀锚定在2%目标附近，不会容忍任何超调，进一步强化了市场对年内再度加息的预期。 IMF的表态恰逢全球债市承压之际。法国10年期国债收益率一度逼近5%，创2002年以来新高，借贷成本已高于希腊和意大利；美国10年期国债收益率攀升至5.28%的数十年高位，即便通胀数据走软也未能遏制抛售势头。在部分市场分析人士看来，日本政策正常化及由此引发的日本资金回流，或是这两场动荡背后不可忽视的结构性力量。 日本央行正常化提速预期升温 日本央行已于今年6月和9月相继加息，将政策利率推升至1.25%，为31年来最高。多数分析师预计年内还将有至少一次加息。 Srinivasan指出，日元疲软进一步推高了原材料进口成本，加剧了国内通胀压力，这也正是促使日本央行持续收紧政策的重要背景之一。日本央行本月晚些时候将召开关键政策会议，市场普遍预计届时利率将维持不变，但可能释放鹰派信号，为12月加息铺路。 此外，中东冲突带来的通胀风险和人工智能需求旺盛，也在本次IMF年会上成为各国政策制定者讨论的重要议题。 IMF：日元干预不违背浮动汇率承诺 在汇率问题上，IMF对日本当局的立场给予背书。Srinivasan表示，日本当局"完全致力于自由浮动汇率制度"，他与日方进行了多次讨论，对此"毫不怀疑"。 IMF在其亚洲经济报告的分析章节中指出，2025年年中以来日元的大幅波动，很大程度上与收益率差等基本面因素关联不大，而是与日元期货的投机性仓位同步移动。日本于今年7月31日与美国联合进行了一次罕见的协调干预，以阻止日元跌至近40年低点。Srinivasan表示，日本汇市深度充足，当局将汇率波动作为"第一道防线"，干预仅在特定情况下使用。 除货币政策外，日本的财政可持续性同样令市场存有疑虑。市场担心日本政府的大规模支出计划，叠加明年4月起为期两年的消费税下调，将进一步扩大本已庞大的债务规模。 Srinivasan承认市场对财政风险的担忧，但也指出，疫情以来日本的财政整合力度实际上已超过其他任何一个G7国家，部分原因在于税收收入的持续增长。他同时强调，日本需要明确新支出和减税计划的资金来源，并建立中期财政框架以稳定市场预期。 日本资金撤离或加剧全球债市波动 全球债市的动荡，与日本政策正常化进程之间的关联正受到越来越多的关注。据彭博专栏作家Gearoid Reidy在分析文章中指出，世界或许并未为"有利率的日本"做好充分准备，而法国可能只是第一个受到冲击的市场。 数据显示，截至今年7月，日本投资者持有约23万亿日元（约合1450亿美元）法国国债，是日本在欧元区最大的超配仓位。然而随着日本10年期国债收益率上月升破3%，创30年新高，经汇率对冲后，法国10年期国债相对日本国债的收益率优势已收窄至约40个基点，吸引力大幅下滑。 收益率优势消退叠加法国财政状况恶化，日本资金已开始松动。数据显示，日本持有的法国国债规模较去年底减少2.5%。三井住友DS资产管理旗下由Shinji Kunibe负责的全球固收基金已出于财政担忧清仓法债。瑞穗的Masayuki Nakajima表示："即便估值看起来更便宜，日本投资者重建仓位的动力也在下降。" 随着IMF为日本加快加息提供政策支撑，日本国内资产吸引力的持续回升，或将使这一趋势延续，并对依赖日本资金的海外债券市场形成持续的结构性压力。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: AI融资成本攀升：Anthropic拟向黑石提供超10%收益率
articles.summary: Anthropic正以远高于市场基准的融资成本推进其史上最大规模芯片融资，折射出AI基础设施军备竞赛背后日益高企的资本代价。 据英国《金融时报》17日报道， Anthropic正向黑石集团（Blackstone）提供逾10%的收益率，以换取后者参与这笔代号"Project North Star"、总规模高达600亿美元的债务融资。 知情人士透露，黑石旗下基金将认购其中90亿美元，约占180亿美元次级贷款的一半，并获得10%的票息，加计新发折价及其他费用后实际总回报更高。 这笔融资规模预计将创下芯片融资历史纪录，并将成为衡量投资者对AI债务胃口的重要风向标。值得关注的是，仅仅四个月前，Anthropic以8.5%利率完成代号"Project Big Sky"的约44亿美元融资，借贷成本的快速攀升，凸显出投资者对AI企业密集融资需求的警惕情绪持续升温。 600亿融资案：规模创纪录，成本同步飙升 "Project North Star"旨在为Anthropic采购约1.5吉瓦由谷歌开发的定制半导体——即张量处理单元（TPU）——提供资金。 整体债务结构分为两层： 约420亿美元为优先级债务，由参与芯片研发的Broadcom提供担保；其余180亿美元为次级贷款，Blackstone认购其中90亿美元，剩余份额将于未来数月面向更广泛投资者出售，出售利率可能低于黑石所获条款。 预计当资金于2027年提款完毕后，这部分债务将进入机构144A债券市场流通。 Blackstone拒绝置评，Anthropic未立即回应置评请求。 溢价逾300个基点，风险溢价需求凸显 根据ICE美银BB级美国高收益债券指数，信用状况与Anthropic相近的借款人在公开债券市场通常支付约7%的收益率。Anthropic此次向黑石提供的10%票息，较该基准高出逾300个基点，若计入折价及费用，实际收益差距更大。 这一溢价反映出两方面压力：其一，投资者对科技企业短期内集中释放的庞大融资需求愈发审慎，要求更高的风险补偿；其二，大型融资交易通常需向锚定投资者和早期承诺方提供额外溢价，以确保交易顺利落地。 借贷成本的快速上行，亦令Anthropic谋求投资级评级的路径更加复杂。评级机构KBRA于今年6月将Anthropic评定为投资级以下一档，本次次级债务预计将获得类似评级。 IPO前的战略布局：高成本融资换长期降费空间 尽管融资成本高企，Anthropic仍选择主动承压，背后存在明确的战略逻辑。据媒体援引知情人士透露，Blackstone已向其投资伙伴表示， 此次交易是在高收益水平下投资Anthropic关联债务的罕见机会——一旦Anthropic完成上市，预计将获得投资级评级，届时其融资成本将大幅下降。 这一叙事本质上是一笔时间套利：Anthropic在上市前以较高利率换取必要的算力储备，并押注上市后信用评级提升将带来再融资空间，从而摊薄长期资本成本。对于黑石等早期投资者而言，则是在风险窗口期锁定高于市场水平的收益。 当前这笔融资既是Anthropic规模扩张的资金保障，也将是AI行业债务融资市场能否持续承接大体量交易的一次关键压力测试。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: AI帮储户多赚钱，银行却慌了：花旗、美银、摩根大通集体对AI Agent设防
articles.summary: 花旗、美国银行和摩根大通相继宣布限制AI智能代理访问客户账户，这场集体设防的背后，是银行业对数万亿美元低成本存款可能被AI"扫走"的深层焦虑。 花旗明确表示， 不允许"第三方AI代理或助手登录客户账户，或直接在其数字银行平台上进行交易"， 称此举旨在保障客户账户与信息安全。美国银行首席执行官Brian Moynihan本周三在接受CNBC采访时表示， 该行正在限制AI代理访问消费者存款账户，同时研究在AI发起支付指令时如何界定责任主体。 摩根大通首席执行官Jamie Dimon则在该行三季度业绩电话会议上表示， 将限制AI代理访问客户账户，理由是"你不会希望出现流氓代理，而且这类代理可能数以千计"。 与此同时，华尔街高管已就消费者使用AI代理进行金融交易的快速增长，与美联储监管人员展开沟通；监管层私下对银行封堵AI代理访问客户账户的举措持欢迎态度。 存款流失威胁利润根基 此次银行业集体行动的直接导火索，是AI个人理财工具的加速涌现。据英国《金融时报》报道， Meta于9月推出Muse AI个人助手后，业界担忧情绪明显升温——市场普遍担心AI代理将自动替消费者将闲置资金从银行账户转移至收益更高的产品。 阿波罗首席经济学家Torsten Slok在一份报告中将这一风险量化：AI助手可能自动将家庭闲置资金从全国平均仅0.1%的活期账户利率，转移至利率达3.3%至5%的账户。报告警告称，"如果每个家庭都使用AI代理优化现金余额收益，银行可能损失大量用于发放贷款的低成本存款，这将对整个金融体系构成威胁。" 摩根大通、美国银行和富国银行目前合计持有1.6万亿美元的无息存款，占其负债总额的16%。若被迫对这部分存款支付3%的利率，三家银行每年将额外承担约470亿美元的成本——相当于其年度税后净利润总和的近一半。 各行表态与责任认定困境 在设防方式上，各行有所差异，但核心逻辑一致：在责任归属尚不明确之前，不允许AI代理自主操作账户资金。 Brian Moynihan明确表示，"我们强烈认为，账户转账授权应有人工参与。"他表示，美国银行正与AI代理服务商沟通，提示其注意消费者可能事后对资金去向产生异议的风险。一位知情人士证实，美国银行已限制AI代理的相关访问权限。 Jamie Dimon则着重强调风险管控逻辑： "我们必须以正确的方式保护客户。我们正在构建相应工具。在此之前，我们不会允许任何外部代理进入公司系统，因为这对客户和摩根大通而言风险太大。" 花旗表示，客户仍可通过特定开放银行服务商授权对账户信息进行有限的只读访问。 据知情人士透露，针对AI代理在金融交易中的合规边界，美联储已与银行业高管展开私下沟通，但美联储拒绝就此置评。 监管层私下对银行限制AI代理访问账户的举措持支持态度，官员认为，消费者如何授权自主技术代其完成金融交易、以及出现问题后的责任认定，可能需要通过立法层面加以厘清。 银行如何应对：让存款"更难流走" 面对AI带来的存款竞争压力，银行业已开始寻求应对之策。咨询公司Simon-Kucher高级合伙人Christoph Stegmeier表示，银行需要通过扩大客户忠诚度计划、优化贷款利率等方式，提升存款产品的黏性。 "你必须让你的存款产品更难被替代，"他说。 这场由AI驱动的存款争夺战，才刚刚开始。银行在技术防线上能坚守多久，以及监管框架能否跟上AI代理的演进速度，将成为决定这场博弈走向的两大关键变量。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 美股最危险的分化：普通股票已经跌惨，AI巨头还能撑多久？
articles.summary: 美股正在上演一场罕见的内部撕裂——指数岿然不动，但指数之下已是一片狼藉。 摩根士丹利首席股票策略师Mike Wilson在最新报告中警告， 收紧的金融条件正在悄然完成美联储的部分工作，只是这一冲击被集中吸收在普通股票身上，而非以AI为核心的少数巨头。 十年期美债收益率突破5.3%，美元升至本轮周期新高，油价居高不下，三重压力叠加之下，摩根士丹利综合金融条件指数已跳升至约1.4个标准差，这一水平在过去35年中仅被突破数次，上一次还是2022年美联储每次会议加息75个基点之时。与此同时，高盛已将预期修正为10月FOMC再加息一次。 市场的关键裂缝已清晰可见：标普500等权重指数在过去六个月落后市值加权指数达6%，9月份当十年期收益率突破5%时，等权重指数单月下跌5%，而市值加权指数几乎持平。高盛Tony Pasquariello虽对"广度崩溃"的论断持部分保留态度，但承认标普500成分股中位数较52周高点已回落15%，为互联网泡沫破裂以来最差读数。两大机构的分歧，恰恰勾勒出当前市场最核心的悬念：这场分化究竟如何收场？ 金融条件已在暗中大幅收紧 表面上，股市指数显得风平浪静。但Wilson指出，真正的收紧早已在水面之下展开。 摩根士丹利构建的综合金融条件指标——综合利率、美元和能源价格的52周Z分数——已攀升至约1.4个标准差，仅次于2022年激进加息周期的水平。这一收紧并非来自单一变量，而是多因素共振：美联储上月将联邦基金利率上调25个基点至3.75%-4.00%，美联储主席沃什援引强劲的劳动力数据、粘性通胀及地缘政治对大宗商品的推涨作为依据；与此同时，十年期美债收益率自2月以来累计上行约130个基点，其中约120个基点来自实际收益率的上升。 Wilson强调，收益率驱动因素的构成至关重要。 历史上，由盈亏平衡通胀预期推动的收益率上行，股市通常能够消化；而由实际收益率主导的上行，则往往对估值构成更直接的压力，这正是当前股债相关性显著转负的原因。 他同时指出，在名义GDP增速接近6%的背景下，十年期收益率维持在5%以上并不反常——2010年代的超低利率才是历史异常，债市不过是在回归均衡。 普通股票已承受真实冲击 收益率上行的代价，正在被普通股票不成比例地消化。 Wilson的广度指标显示，标普500成分股中位于200日均线以上的比例在9月底跌至43%，接近3月下旬44%的低点，此后虽小幅回升至50%，但整体压力未散。标普500远期市盈率也重新测试3月低点附近的约19倍。更值得关注的是，标普500股权风险溢价（远期盈利收益率减去十年期收益率）已跌破零，这一水平自2002年以来几乎未曾出现。 指数层面的"稳定"掩盖了结构性破坏。金融股是另一个预警信号——该板块在30天内下跌7.7%，相对标普500的表现已回落至2019年以来的最低水平。Wilson将金融股的走势视为"近期股市方向最重要的参考指标之一"，在大型银行财报季揭开帷幕之前，该板块能否企稳，将是判断市场走向的关键观察窗口。 这究竟是估值问题还是增长问题？ Wilson认为，目前的冲击仍属估值层面，尚未演变为增长威胁——但这一判断本身存在争议。 支撑其相对乐观立场的数据包括：名义GDP增速刚刚录得8.5%，标普500成分股中位数盈利增速运行在十几个百分点的区间；联邦基金利率与核心CPI之差约为1.4%，"远低于历次衰退前的峰值水平"；10年期与2年期美债收益率利差维持约+45个基点的正斜率，显示市场尚未对衰退进行定价。Wilson据此得出结论， 在上述条件满足的情况下，"历史上12至18个月内罕见出现增长恶化"。 然而，他自己也承认，股权风险溢价降至零同样是历史上的罕见状态。高盛Pasquariello则从另一个维度提示风险：2027年锁定期到期潮或将推动美国股票净供给升至2000年互联网泡沫以来的最高水平，市场的供需格局届时或将承压。 两条收敛路径，哪条更可能发生？ 分歧终将收敛，方向是普通股票追上指数，还是指数向下靠拢普通股票？ Wilson给出了两个触发条件以供观察： 一是金融股企稳，二是衡量美债波动率的MOVE指数回落。 他指出，两者均已出现一定的企稳迹象，但需要更多后续跟进。据彭博，高盛的Rich Privorotsky近日观察到，长端债券隐含波动率已从近期高点回落约30%，为市场提供了一定的喘息空间。 未来数周将是关键检验期。9月CPI数据、沃什在IMF的表态以及10月28日的FOMC会议将相继登场。共识预期显示，受汽油价格环比大涨9.6%影响，9月CPI环比或跳升0.6%，同比升至3.6%。Wilson认为，若CPI核心项温和、沃什承认金融条件收紧已起到部分替代加息的效果，当前的压力有望边际缓解。 但Wilson的多头基案（对应标普500目标点位8300点）与Pasquariello"做空固定收益、做多纳斯达克100指数"的操作逻辑，本质上押注的是两种截然对立的结局。股权风险溢价降至零、广度指标逼近互联网泡沫水平、潜在供给冲击隐现——三者叠加之下，市场对"指数向下收敛"这一尾部风险的准备，或许远远不足。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 林园：现在是乌龟爬着，等牛市哪天爆发，看好AI大时代但不碰个股
articles.summary: 10月15日，林园在私募排排网直播中围绕市场、AI、医药消费等话题分享了自己的判断。 投资作业本课代表整理了要点如下： 1、 我是看好牛市的，我们也是在等牛市。现在是乌龟爬着，等哪天爆发。但具体什么时候有这个东西我也不知道，也是想着平常心，不要整天去想这个事。 2、 我对市场的看法永远是看好，为什么？这就是我的工作。我们没觉得市场下跌或者上涨对我有太大影响。 3、 现在我们也认为AI，就这个行业来判断，它不是终点，现在也是刚刚开始，连一半都还没到，这是我们的判断。 4、我相信现在的AI以后，到最终几十年以后的结局，跟今天互联网走的道路一样。还会有新的东西去取代今天崛起的。 5、房地产本身是个大生意，但具体公司或者什么时候才能走出低迷，我还真不好判断。 6、现在是投资消费这类公司的好时机，估值非常合理。 7、白酒将来股价涨得特别多的时候，股息率可能回到 1% 左右。 8、AI短剧现在很火，我半夜睡不着觉，就不想费眼睛，就听他们来搞笑的东西。这是精神鸦片。 9、在我看来，最后看公司都要看估值，看你的回报。但今天这个时点上，我更加要看一些财务指标。比如手上有现金的、负债少的、未来几年投资小的，我倾向于这些。 林园坚决看好后市和牛市，但强调当前是“乌龟爬着”等爆发的阶段，需要平常心，不预测具体时点；消费和医药经过大幅调整后估值已非常合理，是布局的好时机，尤其围绕老龄化“堰塞湖”带来的慢性病需求成倍增长，他看重有“独门东西”的企业，不等着爆发、提前布局； AI方面他认可这是刚刚开始的大时代，但认为个股竞争格局难以判断，领先企业若干年后能否持续领先全世界都找不到先例，因此只认可买ETF而非个股；选股标准上，他更看重手上现金多、负债少、未来几年投资小的财务指标；此外，粮油龙头因“不管干啥都要吃”而具备长期确定性，乳业总量逻辑未变且已走出最困难时期，中药老字号若有独门产品则“等爆发”那天倍数可观，而美债高息正通过“钱会去比较”的比价效应传导至A股消费股，对投资构成影响。 以下是投资作业本课代表（微信ID：touzizuoyeben）整理的精华内容，分享给大家： 看好AI大时代，不看好个股，为什么？ 主持人：接下来聊聊今天的主题。您在九月的论坛上公开表态看好AI大时代，但紧接着又说依然不投个股。是产业方向对，个股选不出来。 这个选个股的难到底难在哪里？是技术看不懂、看不明白，还是商业模式暂时没办法判断？ 林园：因为AI相对来说是新的东西，创新的东西，这个企业的发展到底最后行不行？这就是我们说的公司，还有多方面因素。但最核心的是你能不能走出来，最后是公司的竞争力。 竞争最后是产品的竞争。如果你走错一步，被别人取代了，或者竞争失去优先性，最后都不行。这是所有企业都存在的问题。那为什么在这方面，这个新的东西又表现得更加淋漓尽致？ 你不能判断今天的领先企业若干年后是否继续领先。全世界基本找不到这样的公司，过去100年没有。当年的领先最后都不会慢，为什么？包括人也是这样，大家说富不过三，一定是有原因的。 但最后我们发现，如果在有限的时间里，最后还是产品需求端，企业是无法判断的。 今天有人说芯片我们的定量是多少年，29年甚至多少年以后，我们都能看到是饱满的。我可以负责任地说，他们说这些话也是拍脑袋的，是以现在的需求来判断未来，这种事遇到很多。 我举一个例子，我们认识一个企业的老总，几年前说我的订单五年内不愁，结果才过了大概两年多时间，我又去问他，他说现在没定的，那些都不做。为什么？ 就是在这个军工企业，以前靠飞机这些，但他给这些提供东西，现在都是无人机了。现代战争一下变化了，这就是需求端有问题。 现在AI突然一下爆发，瓶颈式爆发，大家都要去搞，各路资金也往里边走。当然这种繁荣我们认为是至少现在是真实的。但一旦遇到需求端减弱，资金涌入，生产的东西没有一个人能真正掌握，这个产品最后的数量，这是生意的常识。 这也不是现在AI这个行业，包括农产品。周期怎么来的？都是他判断不了，判断不了几年以后的供应量，更判断不了几年以后的需求，这里边的不确定性太强了。 即使跑出稳定盈利、清晰护城河的AI公司，估值可能比传统行业还低 主持人：假设三五年之后，有几家AI公司真的跑出了稳定盈利、清晰护城河，您会重新把它们纳入研究范围吗？还是说AI这一类题材，您从一开始就打算交给更擅长科技投资的同行？ 林园：那就不是科技企业了，它就是一个正常的企业，回到一个正常问题，可能它的估值比传统行业还低了，完全有可能。 认可买ETF，不买个股 主持人：九月那场论坛上，您也跟刘纪鹏教授罕见地达成一致共识，说想买AI可以买相关ETF。为什么您认可买ETF，但企业依然不买个股？买行业和买企业之间差别到底在哪里？ 林园：差别因为ETF是跟踪一些企业的一揽子东西，它随时都调整。过一段时间这个企业不行了，或者经营不行了，或者股价不行了，反正各种不行了，它就给你踢出了，又排一个新的组合进来。 ETF是一个短期的东西，反正它不断调整，根据不断变化。 当然你认为这个行业确实有大的发展，你买它ETF是有道理，它不断调整，把这种风险可能……对个股的要求就没那么高了，因为有人专门给你做这个。 AI的终局，可能和互联网走的路一样 主持人：互联网崛起的时候，您之前也没有大举参与相关投资。您认为互联网投资跟这一轮AI投资有哪些共同之处？ 林园：都是革命性的东西，从零开始的一些东西。 现在我们也认为AI，就这个行业来判断，它不是终点，现在也是刚刚开始，连一半都还没到，这是我们的判断，大致差不多。 互联网现在已经成熟了，你看全球互联网公司基本就那几家，已经形成规模了。 互联网早期取决于电脑、手机。第一波应该是电脑相关的，PC机，但现在都不存在。 我相信现在的AI以后，到最终几十年以后的结局，跟今天互联网走的道路一样。 还会有新的东西去取代今天崛起的。以前电脑后来被平板取代，被手机取代，这就是互联网的发展历史。现在可能第四代。 AI也差不多，反正都是网络，大同小异，不断叠加，不断取代。看着不是一回事，实际上就是一回事，都是网络的兴起。 我们最早做电脑是IBM、王安，还有更早的那些企业，现在基本都听不到很多声音。后来发展的手机有摩托罗拉、爱立信，中国也出了一大堆，后来就华为，这又是一代。接下来不知道是哪一代。国外也基本都是这个规律。 巴菲特买谷歌不足为奇，只是小比例而已 主持人：那您怎么看待巴菲特买入谷歌呢？ 林园：因为他公司大了，买了一点也不出奇。总有人去参与这个东西，不奇怪。就看人家占的比例，实际上不大。他主要还是巴菲特，主要还是一些传统行业，人家是干实体的，主要资产可能还在实体上。 90年代的长虹，相当于现在的芯片公司，一时风头无两 主持人：请问林总，您90年代买入长虹时的投资思路，和现在对科技股的投资看法是不是不一样？ 林园：那个时候因为我年轻，可以去试。到今天，我们形成的是这么多年的投资经验，再去总结过去，或者发现一些生意的共同东西，成功的、失败的，也在不断总结。 长虹那个时候就相当于现在的芯片公司，那个时候它风头很强，一大堆长虹、康佳、TCL，那时候生产电视机的都很厉害，没有一个企业不赚钱，感觉中国人的钱都被他们挣了。 我感觉当时他们赚钱的总量占了市场很大一部分，按比例的话不比现在这些芯片公司的比例小。 有一次新闻联播播出来四川长虹一种新的模式，跟郑州百文，不知道现在这公司还在不在，那时候也是个明星股。 当时我看到中央台报道我也热血沸腾，我说这不得了，不知道现在这公司还在不在。 以前靠人赚钱，现在靠钱赚钱 主持人：您觉得能总结什么样的公司才能活得长、活得远，最后赚钱活着？会不会随着年龄增长，还有管理规模扩大，跟您年轻时候的决策有所不同？ 林园：原则上我们就是那种拼劲、闯劲。 那个时候的本质就是，非要让我总结这个东西，那个时候是靠人来赚钱的，因为自己没多少钱，靠人的这种不断冲动来赚钱。现在是靠钱来赚钱，还是有区别的。 那个时候人很重要，但现在人也非常重要。但确实是没有那种冲动，这种快乐性没有。以前人是需要工作的，人是需要奋斗的。 这个时候就考虑的问题更多。那个时候不想这些，觉得年轻。现在我看着年轻人我就羡慕，把你年龄给我一点多好。 我对市场永远看好， 涨跌对我影响不大 主持人：在2026年当下，市场热点切换也比较频繁。先请您整体聊聊当前的整体投资框架，跟去年10月排排网路演时的核心判断有没有一些微调？ 林园：我对市场的看法永远是看好，为什么？这就是我的工作。我们没觉得市场下跌或者上涨对我有太大影响。 我们首先看行业的发展，这个行业有没有发展，它的估值到底怎么样。市场现在不是去年10月，我自己没有觉得有明显变化，不会有变化。 现在选公司：倾向手上有现金、负债少、未来几年投资小 主持人：如果今天您重新研究一家上市公司，不考虑目前股价涨跌，您会从哪些方面判断它是不是一家好公司？现在会最先看哪几个条件？ 林园：今天这个时候当然和10年前、20年前、几年前还是有些变化。如果说A股的话，中国确实是供大于求这种局面，商品生产的供大于求，不比前几年有所好转。所以这要求我们做一些事情要更加小心，收缩的状态去处理，不能有一点大意。这就是我们说选股、选公司的标准可能更加苛刻，确实要选那些人。最后不管什么公司，科技公司、传统公司，老灯什么新的都差不多，都是要赚钱，赚不了钱就是麻烦。 在我看来，最后的公司都要看估值，看你的回报。但今天这个时点上，我更加要看一些财务指标。比如手上有现金的、负债少的、未来几年投资小的，我倾向于这些。 房地产是个大生意， 但何时走出低迷不好判断 主持人：林总，您现在对金融行业的看法会不会有变化？比如银行、券商这一类。 林园：银行业务我们没怎么参与。我们总觉得中国银行的市值非常大。 我们就不参与了。就像若干年前我做地产，其实我也不知道地产是最后的结局。但我当时就说，全中国最有钱的公司或者个人，大部分来源于这个，我说这违背常识。违背常识。今天我也这么认为。 主持人：那您现在看来，房地产有没有机会呢？ 林园：房地产应该是个支柱行业，机会肯定有。我相信中国不管是目前还是将来，这一块消费应该占总家庭支出，都是稳稳当当排在第一位。居住没办法改变，人追求美好生活，就是要好房子。 这块本身是个大生意，但具体公司或者什么时候才能走出低迷，我还真不好判断。 现在是投资消费公司最好的时机 主持人：接下来聊聊您最擅长的消费。消费也是您持有很多年的主场。从2021年高点以来，曾经被封为永恒赛道的消费大白马们也震荡了四五年，近期也还在摸底。在您看来，消费调整这么久，目前见底了吗？ 林园：反正我认为现在的估值非常合理。现在是投资消费这类公司的好时机。便宜，从股息率，还有从它的稳定性都可以看到，这个没有问题。 我要强调的是，中国新的有钱人都在所谓的新经济上。不管凭什么富，都是这方面的，这太违背常识了。这不是中国独有现象，全球主要国家都是，这也是不合常理。 我感觉又回到90年代长虹、康佳那种时候，给我的体会实际上差不多。把钱都挣了，而大家都不好过，但他们好过，你看看他们的市值、盈利，动不动上千亿、几千亿，我都觉得吃惊。 未来白酒若涨势凶猛， 股息率可能回到1%左右 主持人： 您去年说过白酒股息率会回到 1%，现在看法有改变吗？ 林园： 我说过这个话，将来股价涨得特别多的时候，股息率可能回到 1% 左右。十年前白酒的股息率就不到 1%，大概 0.8%、0.7% 几，那时候股价低，这几年盈利上来了。现在白酒的股息率大概有 4%，甚至 4% 以上。 龙头企业的股息率如果到 1%，那要涨多少倍？这个变化我相信总有一天会出现。因为我们看到中国的利率走势往下，通缩加剧。至于具体哪天出现，那要等这个板块疯狂、或者大家认同一致的时候。 老龄化下的“堰塞湖”： 医药需求的成倍爆发 主持人： 接下来问问医药。医药也是您长期看好的方向，尤其围绕人口老龄化和慢性病需求。现在慢性病市场空间很大，但医保控费、药品降价、市场竞争也会影响企业利润。您目前在医药板块挑选企业时，最看重哪些条件？ 林园： 还是看疾病本身。实际上医药行业跟现在的 AI 差不多——AI 在各个方面都要用，它就要爆发一下，芯片、硬件、软件都要爆发一下。 疾病也是这样，随着年龄增长，它突然一下。比如高血压，年轻的时候，50 岁以前或者 55 岁以前，吃一点西药基本都能控制住；但到了七八十岁，已经控制不住的话，就需要额外干预。所以如果想象七八十岁的人增加得多的话，这里存在一个堰塞湖，它就会成倍增加。 现在已经有这方面的现象。比如我们开始的慢性病，糖尿病、高血压，最后导致心血管出问题，这些并发症——糖尿病肾病、血压一高肾脏有问题、肝脏也有问题、心血管都有问题。所以这个人口结构，不是我们现在想象的。 另外，这几个月或者过去一年总结出来的那个数据是不准的。我们现在的布局，就是不等着它爆发。 这个研究我们一直在做，比如从 2015 年开始到现在，实际上这些行业的需求和企业的盈利是在增加的。独门生意更适合增长，这就是我们的思路。我是有信心等到这一天。 坚决看好后市 主持人： 目前市场上多空分歧非常大，有观点认为牛市转熊该进入防御，也有观点认为调整就是机会。您对后市大致走向有什么观点？ 林园： 大势判断我不敢说。我们当然看好股市后市，坚决看好。按照现在的估值，我们说看好。 主持人： 近两年来说您的产品净值也备受投资者关注。借着今天直播，您觉得对于目前持有您产品、或者正在考虑配置的投资者，有什么想交流的吗？ 林园： 我就说，这几年我们重点投资的消费、医药（净值）确实是大幅下降、大幅下跌，相比前几年的高位。 但我对我们的产品还是充满信心。 刚才我说生活不痛快，可能也有这方面的因素。但我自己也没去细想。比如年轻的时候感觉到快乐，现在有时候想，为什么我觉得比年轻的时候生活没意思了，可能也有这方面的因素，因为我自己感觉不到。 对我们的产品我还是有信心，没有丝毫改变。现在泡沫还没有挤干净，这也不好。但是我们投资的企业财务指标非常好，未来也不会差。单从财务指标或者投资综合来考虑，我认为我们投资的企业都是非常优秀的。 “不管干啥都要吃”： 粮油龙头的长期确定性 主持人： 接下来问问粮油行业。粮油龙头毛利率低、盈利波动大，人口还在下滑，您为什么依然看好粮油龙头？ 林园： 粮油我看好，是因为不管他干啥都要吃，这种公司长期来说没有问题。 我们作为一个组合的话，我觉得没有什么大的问题，需求量也非常大。按照国外同类公司，他们都能够长大，而且几十年不变，这种企业我们都可以看到。 所以这就是我们投资的思路：我们到底要投今天活得很好、几十年以后或者若干年以后就不在的，还是投一个它还存在，且需求量非常大（的东西）。 当然这个行业也受到了一些挑战，比如人口的问题。但不是针对这个行业，所有行业都会面临。接下来我们投资的一个方向，确实是个短板。凡是牵扯到人的问题，都有问题。 AI 短剧是精神鸦片 主持人： 说到情绪价值，不知道林总对最近的 AI 短剧有没有了解？您对这类传媒行业怎么看？ 林园： AI短剧现在很火，我半夜睡不着觉，就不想费眼睛，就听他们来搞笑的东西。这是精神鸦片。 老年人喜欢瞎扯，喜欢看这方面东西。但最后具体什么时候过劲儿我就不知道了，我相信有一天它会过劲儿的，又会有新的东西出现。 渗透率还在爬坡：乳业的“总量逻辑”没变 主持人： 那接下来再聊聊乳业行业，您怎么看？ 林园： 乳业行业。因为中国人的乳饮、乳品渗透率还是逐年增加，这个行业应该是正常的行业，没有问题。 它总的乳制品消费量，我们觉得数据还是每年在增加。它牛奶的饮用量可能没增加，但牛奶制品、奶茶各种作为补充，总的量还是很稳定，会增加。公司目前的估值也都非常合理。 主持人： 乳制产品也开始同质化，市场竞争愈发激烈，很多渠道商也开始定制乳制品。您怎么看乳制品行业市场竞争越来越激烈的现象？ 林园： 在乳制品行业，这种现象存在多少年了？为什么你看国外的一些品牌基本上都被挤出中国，实际上现在是在头部集中了几家。我相信这些企业的利润会持续向好。 这个行业和别的消费行业还有一点区别，就是它们现在已经走出最困难的时候。 “那是常识”：段永平赌约背后的茅台逻辑 主持人： 林总，您怎么看待段永平之前抛出过一个赌约，他说抱着茅台跟国内任何基金赌一个亿人民币，以十年为限。您怎么看这个赌约？ 林园： 那个赌约是常识，我说是常识，他说的对的。因为你拿着全球第一财务指标好的企业去，那当然大部分是不如他的，这个是正常的，这是常识。 "独门东西”与“等爆发”： 中药老字号的估值博弈 主持人： 我看到有很多投资者也很好奇中药行业。有一些中药老字号估值特别好、又特别多，但渠道又没有跑出来，估值又特别高，股价又在近十年低位，盈利能力没有释放，市值小。这一类企业您看好吗？ 林园： 我看好。就看他有没有独门的东西，这个很重要。就是这些企业的希望，就是刚才我说的等爆发。按照现在的估值，等爆发那一天，他又是多少倍？ 组合新加仓方向 主持人： 还有投资者问到，林总您能不能再说一下组合里有没有新的加仓方向？ 林园： 当然有的是。 主持人： 大概是哪一类行业大方向？ 林园： 就是老龄化。 你别说我是反反复复说的东西，他总有一天会验证的。 现在是乌龟爬着，等牛市哪天爆发 主持人： 林总您还看好后面的牛市吗？依旧坚持 4000 点才是牛市的起点？投资者也想要林总再给大家一点信心。 林园： 我是看好牛市的，我们也是在等牛市。现在是乌龟爬着，等哪天爆发。但具体什么时候有这个东西我也不知道，也是想着平常心，不要整天去想这个事。 这希望是有的，永远是希望。炒股的人也要有希望。人如果没有希望，活着确实少了很多快乐。不要把金钱太当回事。 他们肯定有人去考虑这些资产的倍数，这就是人性。如果美国长期占（据）高利息的话，还是有影响，至少对我的投资有。 “钱会去比较”： 美债高息如何传导到A股消费 主持人： 我们再问一个最近大家都很关心的问题，就是美债收益率。美债收益率如此之高，一旦美债危机爆发，您觉得对 A 股后面会有很大影响吗？ 林园： 已经有影响了。我们消费股起不来，实际上都是那些传导过来的。美国通胀，咱们这边低迷。消费（贷）那么高，美债利息那么高，他自然就会去比较。 我还不如把钱放到银行，去存美债相关的一些东西，肯定有。这个和中国的资产结构有关系，就是少数人掌握了银行储蓄的大头。 他们肯定有人去考虑这些资产的倍数，这就是人性。如果美国长期占（据）高利息的话，还是有影响，至少对我的投资有。 中药未来有几百倍空间 主持人： 您说三大病，中药未来也会有几百倍的空间，您是怎么算出来的？ 林园： 那就是爆发。你现在基本上用的量没有达到正常老龄化增加的速度，最后那个增加的速度会增加很多倍。 来源： 投资作业本Pro ，作者王丽 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 财险反内卷进入深水区：产品新规正式落地，财险行业盈利弹性一触即发？
articles.summary: 10月9日，国家金融监督管理总局发布《财产保险公司保险产品开发管理规定》，于11月1日起施行。此次修订为持续推进的非车险综合治理增加了产品源头约束。保险公司过去依靠渠道费用和条款变通争夺保费的空间收窄，行业承保质量有望进一步改善。 一、发生了什么？——非车险治理延伸至产品源头 1. 产品、费率与责任管理同步收紧： 新规首先对保险产品本身提出了更严格的要求。例如，有些保险产品看似提供了丰富的保障，实际上保障责任很少；还有一些保险公司通过附加险扩大保障范围，却没有相应提高保费，借此争夺客户。新规明确了八类禁止开发的产品情形，并专门规范附加险，要求附加险与主险具有明确关联，防止保险公司利用产品设计变相降价。 其次是规范定价和实际执行。对于已经制定行业示范条款或基准纯风险损失率的险种，保险公司原则上应当采用相关标准；如果采用不同方案，需要说明理由。同时，保险公司不能通过特别约定、批单等方式，私下改变已经审批或备案的保险责任和费率。简单来说，保险公司申报了什么保障、什么价格，实际经营就应按照相应规则执行。 最后是强化内部责任。新规要求保险公司建立由主要负责人牵头的产品管理委员会，明确首席合规官和总精算师的审核责任，并定期评估、清理不再适用的产品。这意味着产品开发、定价和后续管理都将受到更严格的约束，也提高了保险公司通过不规范产品和价格竞争获取业务的成本。 ……
